title: Lesson 1: Understanding Emotions and Emotional Triggers
summary: Emotional intelligence does not mean never feeling upset. It means recognising emotions and triggers, then choosing a professional response.

items.label: Duration
items.body: 45–60 minutes

items.label: Participants
items.body: All Zura Spa staff

items.label: Focus
items.body: Self-awareness, emotional intelligence, recognising triggers, managing reactions and maintaining professionalism

sections.title: 1. Introduction
paragraphs: Imagine two therapists working at Zura Spa.
Both have had a busy day attending to clients.
Towards the end of their shifts, a supervisor approaches them separately and points out that their treatment rooms were not prepared according to the expected standard.

The first therapist immediately becomes defensive. She raises her voice and says: "Why is it always me? Nobody appreciates anything I do here!" She walks away angrily and refuses to listen to the rest of the feedback.

The second therapist also feels disappointed. She has worked hard throughout the day and did not expect to receive a correction. However, she recognises that she is becoming upset. She listens and responds: "I understand. Could you please explain which part of the preparation needs improvement?"
Both therapists experienced an unpleasant emotion. The difference was how they responded to it.

Emotional intelligence does not mean that employees never become angry, disappointed, frustrated or upset. It means recognising emotions and learning to respond appropriately rather than allowing those emotions to control every action.
At Zura Spa, understanding emotions and emotional triggers is essential because employees work closely with clients, colleagues, supervisors and management.
Every employee will experience different emotions at work. The important responsibility is learning how to recognise those emotions and manage their effect on professional behaviour.

sections.title: 2. What are emotions?
paragraphs: Emotions are natural psychological and physical responses to situations, experiences, thoughts and interactions.
They influence how people feel, interpret events and respond to others.
Emotions are not automatically good or bad.
For example, anger may alert an employee that something feels unfair. Anxiety may indicate uncertainty about an important task. Frustration may signal that a process is not working effectively.
However, emotions do not always provide a complete or accurate picture of a situation.
Feeling disrespected does not necessarily mean someone intended to disrespect you.
Feeling criticised does not always mean you are being personally attacked.
An emotion is real, but the interpretation attached to it may need to be examined.

items.label: Happiness
items.body: Feeling pleased or satisfied.

items.label: Anger
items.body: Feeling upset about something perceived as wrong.

items.label: Fear
items.body: Feeling concerned about possible danger or consequences.

items.label: Sadness
items.body: Feeling disappointed or experiencing loss.

items.label: Frustration
items.body: Feeling blocked or unable to achieve an expected result.

items.label: Embarrassment
items.body: Feeling uncomfortable about how others may perceive you.

items.label: Anxiety
items.body: Feeling worried or uncertain.

items.label: Pride
items.body: Feeling satisfied with an achievement.

sections.title: 3. What is emotional intelligence?
paragraphs: Emotional intelligence is the ability to recognise, understand and manage one's emotions while responding thoughtfully to the emotions of others.
In the workplace, emotional intelligence helps employees maintain professional relationships and make better decisions.

items.label: 1. Self-awareness
items.body: Recognising what you are feeling and understanding how those emotions influence your behaviour.

items.label: 2. Self-regulation
items.body: Managing emotional reactions rather than responding impulsively.

items.label: 3. Personal responsibility
items.body: Choosing actions that support professional standards, even when emotions are uncomfortable.

items.label: 4. Empathy
items.body: Making an effort to understand another person's perspective without automatically assuming you know how they feel.

items.label: 5. Relationship management
items.body: Communicating respectfully, resolving disagreements and maintaining productive workplace relationships.

sections.title: 4. What are emotional triggers?
paragraphs: An emotional trigger is something that produces a noticeable emotional reaction.
A trigger may be a situation, statement, behaviour, memory or expectation.
Different people may respond differently to the same trigger.
For example, one employee may receive correction and feel motivated to improve. Another may feel embarrassed or rejected. A third may become defensive because of a previous unpleasant experience.
The correction is the event, but each employee's interpretation and emotional response may differ.
Recognising a trigger does not mean that the employee is weak. It means becoming more aware of the situations that influence personal reactions.

sections.title: 5. Understanding the connection between events, thoughts, emotions and actions
paragraphs: Employees sometimes believe that another person's behaviour automatically determines their own response.
However, there is often an important step between an event and a reaction: how the employee interprets what happened.
Event: What happened. Thought: What I believe it means. Emotion: What I feel. Action: What I do.

Important: Not every concern is a misunderstanding. Sometimes employees are genuinely treated unfairly. Emotional intelligence includes recognising real problems and addressing them through appropriate channels.

sections.title: Example: Receiving correction
paragraphs: Event: A supervisor says that the treatment room was not properly prepared.
Thought: "She thinks I'm incompetent." Emotion: Embarrassment and anger. Action: The employee argues and refuses to listen.
Now consider a different interpretation of the same event.

Thought: "There may be something I need to improve. Let me understand the concern." Emotion: The employee may still feel disappointed but is less likely to react defensively. Action: She asks questions and takes appropriate corrective action.
The situation has not changed, but the employee's interpretation and response have changed.

sections.title: 6. Recognising the early signs of emotional reactions
paragraphs: Emotions often produce physical, mental and behavioural signs.
Learning to recognise these signs can help employees respond before their emotions become overwhelming.
These signs vary from person to person and are not proof of any particular emotion.
Ask yourself: "What usually happens to my voice, face, thoughts and behaviour when I become upset?"
Recognising your own early signs gives you an opportunity to choose a more constructive response.

sections.title: Physical signs
list: Faster heartbeat.
Muscle tension.
Tightness in the chest or stomach.
Sweating.
Shallow or rapid breathing.
Feeling unusually restless.
Headaches or fatigue.

sections.title: Mental signs
list: Repeatedly thinking about an upsetting situation.
Assuming the worst.
Difficulty concentrating.
Feeling personally attacked.
Wanting to prove someone wrong immediately.
Finding it difficult to consider another explanation.

sections.title: Behavioural signs
list: Raising your voice.
Interrupting others.
Rolling your eyes.
Slamming objects.
Walking away angrily.
Sending impulsive messages.
Becoming unusually withdrawn.
Responding sarcastically.

sections.title: 7. Common emotional triggers at Zura Spa
A. Receiving correction from a supervisor
paragraphs: An employee may feel embarrassed when a mistake is pointed out.
Unhelpful reaction: "You always find something wrong with my work!"
Professional response: "I understand the concern. Please, can you explain what I should do differently?"

sections.title: B. A colleague failing to complete a task
paragraphs: An employee may become frustrated when another person's incomplete work affects her responsibilities.
Unhelpful reaction: "You're so lazy! You never do anything properly."
Professional response: "I noticed the room is not fully prepared. Was there a difficulty? We need to resolve it before the client arrives."

sections.title: C. A difficult client interaction
paragraphs: A client may speak impatiently or express dissatisfaction.
Unhelpful reaction: "If you don't like it, that's your problem."
Professional response: "I understand that you're dissatisfied. Could you explain what happened so we can determine the appropriate next step?"
Professionalism does not require employees to tolerate threats or abuse. Such situations should be handled according to appropriate safety and reporting procedures.

sections.title: D. Feeling overlooked
paragraphs: An employee may feel disappointed when another colleague receives recognition.
Unhelpful reaction: "Management only appreciates certain people."
Professional response: "I would appreciate feedback on my performance and what I can do to improve."

sections.title: E. Unexpected changes to responsibilities
paragraphs: An employee may feel overwhelmed when an additional task is assigned.
Unhelpful reaction: "Why is everybody always disturbing me?"
Professional response: "I'm currently handling another assignment. Could you help me clarify which task should take priority?"

sections.title: 8. The difference between feeling an emotion and acting on it
paragraphs: Employees should understand that experiencing an emotion does not automatically justify every behaviour that follows.
The goal is not to stop employees from feeling emotions. It is to help them choose behaviour that remains professional.
table: Explaining the difficulty and seeking a solution
Reporting the issue and seeking guidance

sections.title: 9. Managing emotional triggers in the moment
list: Step 1: Recognise the emotion. Identify what you are feeling. Naming an emotion can help create awareness.
Step 2: Avoid reacting immediately. Where safe and practical, pause, slow your breathing or choose not to send an emotional message immediately.
Step 3: Examine your interpretation. What actually happened? What am I assuming? Could there be another explanation? Do I have enough information? What outcome do I want?
Step 4: Choose a professional response. Focus on communicating the concern rather than attacking the person.
Step 5: Seek support when necessary. If the situation is too difficult to handle effectively, request appropriate assistance or supervisor support.

items.label: P — Pause before reacting
items.body: Avoid immediate responses driven by strong emotion.

items.label: A — Acknowledge the emotion
items.body: Recognise whether you are angry, frustrated, anxious, disappointed or embarrassed.

items.label: U — Understand the trigger
items.body: Identify what happened and separate facts from assumptions.

items.label: S — Select an appropriate response
items.body: Choose words and actions that address the situation constructively.

items.label: E — Engage professionally
items.body: Communicate respectfully, seek clarification or escalate appropriately.

sections.title: PAUSE example
paragraphs: A therapist receives a message that her next appointment has been moved.
She feels irritated because she had already arranged her schedule.
Using PAUSE, she recognises the frustration, checks the actual appointment details and asks reception to clarify the updated plan.
Instead of reacting angrily, she communicates the operational concern and adjusts her responsibilities appropriately.

sections.title: 11. Understanding the emotions of others
paragraphs: Emotional intelligence also involves recognising that colleagues and clients may be experiencing emotions that are not immediately obvious.
Employees should avoid making definite judgments about other people's emotions based only on facial expressions or body language.
Instead of assuming: "You're angry with me." Ask: "Is there something you would like us to clarify?"
Instead of: "Why are you being so difficult?" Ask: "Could you explain what is concerning you?"
Empathy involves making room for another person's perspective, not claiming to know exactly what they feel.
list: A colleague may be quiet because she is concentrating.
A client may be impatient because she has been waiting longer than expected.
A new employee may ask repeated questions because she is uncertain about a procedure.
A supervisor may appear serious because an operational issue requires attention.

sections.title: 12. Emotional intelligence during workplace disagreements
paragraphs: Disagreements are normal when people work together.
However, employees should avoid allowing personal emotions to turn professional differences into personal attacks.

sections.title: Example — cleaning a treatment room
paragraphs: Two therapists disagree about responsibility for cleaning a treatment room.
One therapist says: "You never do your work properly." The other responds: "You're always looking for trouble." The disagreement becomes personal.

Better approach — Therapist A: "I noticed the room was not ready after the previous session. Can we clarify who was responsible for completing the preparation?" Therapist B: "I understood that the next shift would handle it. Let's confirm the procedure with the supervisor."
The employees focus on the issue rather than attacking each other.

sections.title: Useful habits during disagreements
list: Speak about specific behaviour rather than someone's character.
Avoid absolute statements such as "you always" or "you never."
Listen before defending yourself.
Ask questions instead of assuming intentions.
Maintain appropriate boundaries.
Seek supervisor support when necessary.

sections.title: 13. Emotional triggers and workplace WhatsApp communication
paragraphs: Digital communication can make emotional reactions more difficult to manage because written messages may be misunderstood.

An employee may receive a short message: "See me when you arrive." She immediately assumes she is in trouble. She becomes anxious and discusses the message with colleagues. However, the supervisor may simply want to provide an update.
Better approach: "Good afternoon. I received your message. Is there anything I should prepare before we meet?"
Employees should avoid using WhatsApp to express anger impulsively, embarrass colleagues or prolong disagreements.

sections.title: Before sending an emotional message
list: Am I responding to facts or assumptions?
Am I upset right now?
Would I use these words in a respectful face-to-face conversation?
Is the staff group the appropriate place for this concern?
Would a private conversation be more effective?

sections.title: 14. Emotional intelligence does not mean suppressing genuine concerns
paragraphs: Employees should not misunderstand emotional intelligence as a requirement to remain silent when something is wrong.
A professional employee can express disappointment, frustration or disagreement respectfully.

An employee who believes she has been assigned an unreasonable workload should not pretend that everything is fine. She can communicate constructively: "I'm finding it difficult to complete the current assignments within the available time. Could we review the priorities or discuss additional support?"
Similarly, employees should be able to raise concerns about unfair treatment, harassment, unsafe conditions or inappropriate behaviour through suitable channels.
Emotional intelligence is not about accepting every situation without question. It is about communicating and responding thoughtfully while protecting legitimate boundaries.

sections.title: Case study A: The correction that caused anger
paragraphs: A supervisor points out that a therapist did not follow the expected room-preparation procedure.
The therapist feels embarrassed and immediately raises her voice. She refuses to listen to the explanation.
Expected lesson: Employees can recognise uncomfortable emotions and still respond professionally to feedback.
list: What emotion may the therapist have experienced?
What triggered the emotional reaction?
How did her response affect communication?
How could she apply the PAUSE method?
How should the supervisor deliver correction respectfully?

sections.title: Case study B: The colleague who received praise
paragraphs: During a staff meeting, one employee receives recognition for excellent performance.
Another employee feels disappointed because she believes her own efforts have not been noticed. She begins speaking negatively about the recognised colleague.
Expected lesson: Employees should manage disappointment without undermining colleagues.
list: What emotions may be involved?
Why might the employee feel overlooked?
Is the colleague receiving praise responsible for those feelings?
What would be a more constructive response?
How can management support fair and transparent recognition?

sections.title: Case study C: The impatient client
paragraphs: A client arrives for a massage appointment and becomes frustrated because of a delay.
She speaks impatiently to the receptionist. The receptionist feels personally attacked and responds sharply.
Expected lesson: Employees should acknowledge client concerns without allowing frustration to control their behaviour.
list: What emotional triggers affected both people?
How could the receptionist respond professionally?
What information should be communicated to the client?
When should a supervisor assist?
What boundaries should be maintained if the client becomes abusive?

sections.title: Case study D: The misunderstood message
paragraphs: A supervisor sends an employee a brief WhatsApp message requesting a meeting.
The employee assumes the meeting is disciplinary. She becomes anxious and starts complaining to colleagues.
Later, she discovers the meeting concerns a training opportunity.
Expected lesson: Emotional reactions may be influenced by interpretations that have not been verified.
list: What was the triggering event?
Which part of the employee's reaction was based on an assumption?
What question could she have asked?
How can employees manage uncertainty?
How can supervisors communicate requests more clearly?

sections.title: 16. Practical group activity: Identify the trigger
paragraphs: Activity duration: 10 minutes.
Purpose: Help employees recognise emotional triggers and practise choosing professional responses.
Divide participants into pairs or small groups. For each situation, identify the possible emotion, trigger, unhelpful reaction and professional alternative.
Expected outcome: Participants should recognise that emotions are natural but professional responses can be developed through awareness and practice.
table: Congratulate the colleague and seek feedback on your own progress
A client complains about a delay
Acknowledge the concern and explain the next step
Confirm the change and clarify priorities
A colleague does not greet you

sections.title: Reflection questions
list: Which situations are most likely to trigger strong emotions?
What signs help you recognise that you are becoming upset?
How can you respond without attacking others?
When would it be appropriate to request support?

sections.title: 17. Interactive assessment
paragraphs: Complete the Lesson 1 Knowledge Check at the bottom of this lesson. Choose an option, give your reason, then submit.
list: What is emotional intelligence in the workplace? Never experiencing anger or frustration / Recognising and managing emotions while responding thoughtfully to others / Always agreeing with colleagues and supervisors

A supervisor corrects your work and you feel embarrassed. What is the most professional response? Listen, seek clarification and respond appropriately / Immediately argue to protect your reputation / Refuse to discuss the correction

Which statement best describes an emotional trigger? A rule that employees must follow / Proof that another person intended to offend you / A situation or experience that produces an emotional reaction

What should you do when you notice that you are becoming angry? Send an immediate message expressing everything you feel / Pause, recognise the emotion and consider an appropriate response / Assume the other person is deliberately provoking you

Does emotional intelligence mean remaining silent about unfair treatment? No. Concerns can be communicated respectfully through appropriate channels / Yes. Professional employees must never express disagreement / Yes. Employees should accept every instruction without question

sections.title: 18. Personal assignment
paragraphs: Each employee should answer the following questions in writing.
list: Explain what emotions are and why they are a normal part of workplace life.
Define emotional intelligence in your own words.
Identify five common emotional triggers in a workplace.
Describe three physical or behavioural signs that may indicate you are becoming upset.
Explain the difference between experiencing anger and acting aggressively.
Describe the PAUSE method and how you can apply it at work.
Explain how assumptions can influence emotional reactions.
Describe a situation in which emotional intelligence could improve teamwork at Zura Spa.
Identify three emotional triggers you would like to manage more effectively.
Explain how an employee can communicate genuine dissatisfaction without becoming disrespectful.

sections.title: 19. Seven-day emotional awareness challenge
table: Identify the emotions you experience during your workday
Recognise one situation that commonly triggers frustration
Practise pausing before responding when upset
Separate an event from your interpretation of it
Respond constructively to a correction or unexpected change
Practise empathy during a conversation with a colleague or client
Reflect on how emotional awareness influenced your behaviour

sections.title: 20. Final lesson and takeaway
paragraphs: Every employee experiences emotions.
Some days may be enjoyable and productive. Other days may involve disappointment, frustration, uncertainty or unexpected challenges.
At Zura Spa, employees should learn to recognise their emotions without allowing those emotions to determine every response.
Understanding emotional triggers helps employees avoid unnecessary conflict, receive feedback more effectively, communicate concerns responsibly and maintain positive workplace relationships.
Professionalism does not require employees to pretend that they never feel upset.
It requires developing the ability to respond thoughtfully, respectfully and responsibly.
Next topic: Managing Anger and Frustration Professionally.

remember: Your emotions are part of being human, but they do not have to control your behaviour. Learn to recognise what you feel, understand what triggers your reactions and choose responses that reflect professionalism and respect. At Zura Spa, emotional intelligence helps us communicate better, support one another and create a workplace where challenges are handled with maturity rather than unnecessary conflict.
